1.pericope_label: And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins; Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience: Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others.

schools.summary: Distinguish the two nouns as a climax rather than a repetition: the first signifies a swerving aside and a falling, the second an entire missing of the mark, so that even in the plural the second denotes positive principles of evil doing while the first points to failure in particular acts by men not necessarily out of the right way; note also that a later verse in the same passage carries only one of the two. Take the phrase about the prince of the power of the air as unique and difficult, and resolve it in two steps — it means not a power over the air but a power dwelling in the region of the air, and the word for power is used almost technically in this epistle of superhuman power considered collectively, so that the Evil One rules such power. Supply the physics behind the term for air, which the ancients used of the lower and denser atmosphere over against another word for the higher and rarer; and observe that whoever denies a personal devil cannot successfully deny the crime waves of modern men. Then separate the two words rendered world, one naming the appointed period and the other the material and sensuous character of things, so that the former life is at once transitory and carnal.

Divide the two nouns by nation instead of by degree, taking sins to be spoken chiefly of the Gentiles who knew not God and trespasses of the Jews who had the law and yet disregarded it. Describe the power of the air as unspeakably penetrating and widely diffused, while holding that as to its baneful influence it is beneath the orb of believers. Take the word for age as a long succession of corrupt generations rather than the material frame of things. On the metaphor of death itself, report that all writers and all nations employ it to express extreme misery, and read the legal sense as primary here: having sinned they were condemned and might be considered dead in law, incapable of any legal act and liable at any moment to a punishment already deserved.

Open by distinguishing two deaths. The bodily one carries no crime and no peril, being a matter of nature rather than of deliberate choice, taking its origin in the transgression of the first man and passing thence into a nature, and in any case shortly brought to an end; the spiritual one, being a matter of choice, has criminality and has no termination. Add a remark on the writer's manner: having said that they had arrived at the very last degree of wickedness, he takes care not to distress them excessively, since men are put to shame when their former misdeeds are brought forward even after those deeds are cancelled.

Divide the state into two and keep both. Sinners are dead in state, destitute of the principles and powers of spiritual life and cut off from God who is the fountain of it; and they are dead in law, as a condemned malefactor is called a dead man. Decline the fine distinction between the two nouns and take the pair for all sorts of sin, habitual and actual, of heart and of life.

Insist that this is no danger of death but a real and present one, so that the state described is not exposure to ruin but ruin already in possession. Report that classical writers used the same metaphor, though never of spiritual death, of which they knew nothing, but of the absence of moral principle, and cite the Stoic who told his hearers that the instructor is dead and they are dead. Then refuse two common glosses on the word for age: it does not mean the course God ordained, nor the elements of the world, but the depravity that pervades the whole of it.

debates.question: Do trespasses and sins differ, and how?

sides.position: They form a climax: the first is a swerving aside and falling, the second an entire missing of the mark, so that the second denotes positive principles of evil doing
They divide by nation: sins spoken chiefly of the Gentiles who knew not God, trespasses of the Jews who had the law and disregarded it
No distinction is to be pressed; the pair stands for all sorts of sin, habitual and actual, of heart and of life
Only that both stand here where a later verse in the passage has one

debates.question: In what sense were they dead?

sides.position: Dead in state, destitute of the principles and powers of spiritual life, and dead in law as a condemned malefactor is called a dead man
Chiefly in law: having sinned they were condemned, incapable of any legal act and liable at any moment to a punishment already deserved
Really and presently dead, not merely in danger of death
Spiritually dead as distinct from bodily death, the one a matter of choice and therefore criminal and unending, the other a matter of nature and shortly ended

debates.question: What does the course of this world mean?

sides.position: A long succession of corrupt ages
Not the course God ordained, nor the elements of the world, but the depravity that pervades the whole of it
The appointed period, set beside a second word naming the material and sensuous character of things, so that the former life was at once transitory and carnal

outliers.note: Alone reads the passage as a matter of pastoral tact, noticing that having charged them with the last degree of wickedness the writer takes care not to distress them further, since men are shamed by misdeeds recalled even after those deeds are cancelled.

Alone supplies the physics behind the word for air, the lower and denser atmosphere as against the higher and rarer, and alone turns the doctrine on the present day by remarking that whoever denies a personal devil cannot successfully deny the crime waves of modern men.

themes: the prince of the power of the air
children of wrath, even as others

4.pericope_label: But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;) And hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus: That in the ages to come he might shew the exceeding riches of his grace in his kindness toward us through Christ Jesus.

schools.summary: Call the word rich a beautiful expression and turn it on the reader's own values: men are often rich in gold and silver and pride themselves on it, but mercy is the wealth of God, and he is so rich in it that he can make all blessed. Observe that the idea of richness — in grace, in glory, in mercy — is especially frequent in this epistle, and list the places. Press what the love was shown toward: love to the children of wrath, love to those who had no love to return; a man loves his friend and his benefactor, while God loves his foes and seeks to do them good. On the clause about being dead, argue that the resurrection of the head made that of the members certain, as though the whole body were raised together, and that the entrance of our representative into heaven is the pledge of ours. Note that the pronoun shifts here from you Gentiles to us. Add the purpose clause: the conversion of such sinners is to stand as a perpetual encouragement to others.

Grant frankly that these blessings are not yet seen by mortal eyes and that as respects ourselves salvation is still the object of hope; then hold that in Christ we already possess a blessed immortality, since what has hitherto appeared only in the head belongs truly to the members by the secret union, and of everything we now want we have a sure pledge and foretaste in his person. Collect the classical parallels for the metaphor of riches, since the best writers use rich and riches in this way, one speaking of the riches of philosophy and the Roman orator of the riches of the mind, meaning the excellencies of understanding and virtue. Distinguish the mercy that is general and providential toward all men from the special mercy exhibited only in Christ, and explain the epithet by the freedom and liberality of the dispensing, the number of the recipients and the variety of the channels — covenant, mission, redemption, regeneration, pardon, salvation — while it remains inexhaustible. Allow the raising to be read either of the spiritual resurrection or of the bodily one, called already accomplished because it is certain and because the people rose in their representative.

Order love and mercy so that neither is lost: make infinite love the groundwork, which in reference to us assumes the form of mercy, and mercy in turn provides the Saviour. Then mark the tense plainly, calling the sitting together spoken by way of anticipation, since believers are not yet possessed of their seats though each has a place prepared.

Separate love and mercy by their object rather than merging them: love is God's inclination to do us good considered simply as creatures, mercy regards us as apostate and miserable, and the eternal good-will is the fountain from which every mercy proceeds.

debates.question: What does the clause about being dead in sins attach to?

sides.position: To the loving: God did not quicken us while we were dead, but loved us then and made provision
To the quickening, since he brought life out of spiritual death

debates.question: How can the raising and the sitting be spoken of as already done?

sides.position: By the secret union with the head, so that what has appeared only in him belongs truly to the members, though as respects ourselves salvation is still the object of hope
By the closeness of the connection, the resurrection of the head making that of the members certain and our representative's entrance the pledge of ours
By anticipation, believers not being yet possessed of their seats though each has a place prepared
Either of the spiritual resurrection, or of the bodily one reckoned already accomplished because certain

debates.question: How do love and mercy stand to one another?

sides.position: Love regards us simply as creatures, mercy as apostate and miserable, the eternal good-will being the fountain of every mercy
Infinite love is the groundwork, which in reference to us assumes the form of mercy, and mercy provides the Saviour
The point is not the order but the object: love to the children of wrath, to those who had no love to return

outliers.note: Alone divides mercy into the general and providential sort shown to all men and the special sort exhibited only in Christ, and grades the epithet rich by the freedom of the dispensing, the number of recipients and the variety of channels.
Alone attaches the clause about being dead in sins to the quickening rather than to the loving, against the reading that God loved us while we were dead and made provision then.

themes: God, who is rich in mercy
made us sit together in heavenly places

8.pericope_label: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.

schools.summary: Settle the antecedent of the pronoun on grammatical grounds and say so plainly: the pronoun is neuter while the word for faith is feminine, so it points not to faith but to the salvation by grace just described, which is the obvious interpretation and now generally conceded. Add that the word for grace is feminine too, so the pronoun refers to neither, but to the act of being saved by grace on the condition of faith. Record who is reported on the other side — Doddridge, Beza, Piscator and Chrysostom among them — while calling the point theologically small. Distinguish two formulas commonly treated as identical: justification by faith names one completed act, salvation by grace a continuous state lasting till the judgment, and the latter suits this epistle better, since its whole idea is the continuous indwelling in Christ; note the wording answers almost verbally to Peter's speech at the council in Jerusalem. Take the word for workmanship from the verb for making with an ending denoting result, used here not of the original creation but of moral and spiritual renewal, though the noun occurs elsewhere only of God's works in creation. Offer for the clause on good works the rendering on the basis or condition of good works, the works being future in themselves yet contemplated as already existent in God's foreknowledge; and call the following clause perhaps the strongest expression in all scripture of the mystery of predestination, since it covers not merely call and regeneration but the very works in which free will is most plainly exercised.

Set out the Greek and reach the same verdict as the others, that the neuter pronoun cannot stand for the feminine noun but has the whole preceding sentence for its antecedent; say simply that it covers the whole clause. Then hold the line from the other side on the good works: we are not saved for good works but saved in order to perform them.

Set the two halves of the sentence against each other as a division of labour. On God's side salvation is unmixed grace, since he declares he owes us nothing and it is no reward or recompense; on man's side the only question is how the offered thing is received, and the answer is by faith, which strips us of all commendation and brings a man empty to God that he may be filled. Draw the polemical conclusion: we ought to be silent about free will, good intentions, fancied preparations, merits and satisfactions, each of which claims a share of the praise. Compress the argument of two whole epistles into three phrases — that righteousness comes from the mercy of God alone, is offered in Christ by the gospel, and is received by faith without the merit of works. Then turn the workmanship clause against opponents phrase by phrase: the apostle does not say we are assisted, nor that the will is prepared and then left to run by its own strength, nor that the power of choosing rightly is bestowed and the choice left to us, but that we are God's work.

debates.question: What is the antecedent of the pronoun in and that not of yourselves?

sides.position: Not faith, since the pronoun is neuter and the noun feminine, but the salvation by grace just described
Neither faith nor grace, both being feminine, but the act of being saved by grace on the condition of faith
The whole preceding clause

debates.question: Who read the pronoun of faith, and did the Greek fathers?

sides.position: Doddridge, Beza, Piscator and Chrysostom are named among those referring it to faith, though the point is theologically small
Chrysostom with Theodoret and Theophylact held the contrary, Theophylact saying that not faith but being saved by faith is the gift

debates.question: Are justification by faith and salvation by grace the same formula?

sides.position: No: the first names one completed act, the second a continuous state lasting till the judgment, and the second suits this epistle better
They are two sides of one division of labour, unmixed grace on God's part and simple reception on man's

debates.question: What relation do the good works bear to the salvation?

sides.position: They are the basis or condition on which we are created, future in themselves yet contemplated as already existent in God's foreknowledge
We are not saved for good works but saved in order to perform them
The clause excludes assistance, preparation of the will and bestowed power of choice alike, since we are simply God's work

outliers.note: Alone drives a wedge between justification by faith and salvation by grace, making the one a completed act and the other a continuous state, and alone renders the clause on good works as naming their basis or condition rather than their purpose.

Alone prints the Greek fathers on the opposite side of the pronoun question from the side another commentator assigns them, quoting Theophylact that not faith but being saved by faith is called the gift.

themes: by grace are ye saved through faith
not of works, lest any man should boast

11.pericope_label: Wherefore remember, that ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh, who are called Uncircumcision by that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh made by hands; That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world: But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.

schools.summary: Turn the command to remember into a recommendation of the faculty itself: no power of the mind can be better employed to produce humility, penitence, gratitude and love than the memory, and it is well to recall former sins and dwell on our hardness of heart until the heart is affected. On the two party names, hear contempt in the verb — that both sides are said to be called by their titles implies the names were now mere names and virtually nothing — and collect the other forms the same denial takes, circumcision set against obedience to God's commandments, against faith working by love, against the new creation, against the unity of all in Christ; find in the added phrase about hands a contrast between a carnal circumcision belonging to the unbelieving and a spiritual one belonging to Christians. Note that the abstract nouns are used to describe the two peoples, and that the word for made by hands is a verbal adjective agreeing with the second. Read the catalogue of losses as one root and two branches: the condition is summed up in being separate from Christ, from which follow the loss of the covenant and the loss of hope and of God in the world, since Christ is at once the substance of Israel's covenant and the revealer of God. Press one word — the text says not aliens but alienated, implying the covenant was the true birthright of humanity from which mankind had fallen. Note that the word for commonwealth occurs only twice in the New Testament and that the term for godless means both being without God and hostility to him; and explain far off and near from Jewish usage about access to the temple.

Take the missing sign more gravely than the others: circumcision was the token distinguishing God's people and its absence the mark of a profane person, and since God usually connects his grace with the sacraments the want of them is taken as evidence that his grace was wanting too — but add at once that the argument does not hold universally. Argue the dependence of everything on the one promise, since all the promises hang on that made to Abraham and lose their value without it, so that to take away the covenant of salvation is to leave no hope. Give three ends for the command to remember: to magnify the grace of God in their conversion, to humble them by a view of their former state, and to teach them that they could never be saved by works of their own.

Explain why the command to remember was needed at all: when men are raised from great meanness to corresponding or greater dignity it is usual with one and all not so much as to retain any recollection of their former condition, being nourished in the new glory. Notice the rhetorical management as well, that the writer lowers the advantages of the one party and admires the disadvantages of the other, arguing with each according to their character.
Read the taunt sociologically: hypocritical professors value themselves chiefly on external privileges and reproach those destitute of them.
Add to the ends of remembering that they may ever see and feel their obligation to live a pure life; and explain far off and near from Jewish usage about access to the temple.

debates.question: Why is the command to remember given?

sides.position: Because men raised from meanness to dignity commonly retain no recollection of their former condition, being nourished in the new glory
Because no power of the mind produces humility, penitence, gratitude and love so well as memory
To magnify the grace of God, to humble them by a view of their former state, and to teach them that works could never save them
That they may ever see and feel their obligation to live a pure life

debates.question: What weight has the taunt of Uncircumcision?

sides.position: Contempt on both sides: the verb implies the names were now mere names and virtually nothing
It shows how hypocritical professors value themselves on external privileges and reproach those destitute of them

It is graver than that: circumcision was the token distinguishing God's people, and since God connects his grace with the sacraments the want of them was taken as evidence his grace was wanting — though the argument does not hold universally

debates.question: How are the losses catalogued in the passage related?

sides.position: One root and two branches: separation from Christ, from which follow the loss of the covenant and the loss of hope and of God in the world
They hang on the promise to Abraham, all promises losing their value without it, so that to take away the covenant is to leave no hope

outliers.note: Alone accounts for the command to remember by the psychology of sudden advancement, and alone comments on the writer’s handling of the two parties, lowering the advantages of the one and admiring the disadvantages of the other.
Alone presses that the text says not aliens but alienated, drawing from the participle the claim that the covenant was the true birthright of humanity from which mankind had fallen.

themes: Gentiles in the flesh, called Uncircumcision
aliens from the commonwealth of Israel
made nigh by the blood of Christ

14.pericope_label: For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us; Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace; And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby: And came and preached peace to you which were afar off, and to them that were nigh. For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father.

schools.summary: Insist on the pronoun: it is he himself who is our peace, not merely what he did, necessary as that was. Make the same point by comparison — the Old Testament promises a prince of peace and the Lord elsewhere gives peace, but here alone he is called not the giver but the peace itself, his own nature being the actual tie of unity between God and mankind and between man and man. Warn that a double meaning runs through the whole passage, peace between Jew and Gentile and peace between both and God, and that it is not always easy to tell which branch a given expression belongs to; suggest comparing the parallel in Colossians, where only the second branch appears. Give the archaeology of the middle wall: a partition in the temple courts divided the court of the Gentiles from the court of Israel with an inscription forbidding a Gentile to go further, and there was an uproar when the apostle was accused of taking a Greek past it; note that the compound noun is very rare anywhere, known from one papyrus and one inscription. Admit the grammar of the next clause is unsettled, the enmity standing in apposition either to the wall of partition or to the law of commandments, and weigh whether in his flesh belongs to the breaking down or to the abolishing. Press the verb for abolishing, which elsewhere means to supersede by something better, so that the law is abolished as a law in ordinances, that is in the letter, and established in the spirit; and observe that nobody would say of a mere moral teacher that he accomplished a result by his flesh.
Make the middle wall the ceremonial law itself, so called by allusion to the partition in the temple.

Turn the title into an assurance and a rebuke at once: let no one who dwells in Christ doubt that he is reconciled to God, and let the Jews who despised that grace while boasting themselves the holy people observe that if Christ is the peace, then all who are outside him are at variance with God. Illustrate the abolished marks by a contemporary parallel — circumcision, sacrifices, washings and forbidden foods distinguished Israel as the white and the red cross distinguish the French from the Burgundians, and a prince uniting two contending nations would remove the badges of their former enmity. Then give the mechanism plainly: the Son of God, by assuming a nature common to all, formed in his own body a perfect unity.

Doubt that the allusion to the temple partition is so precise, and take the expression of the whole distinction that Jewish laws and customs made; report the alternative that it refers to their ancient practice of living apart with a river or a wall between themselves and their heathen neighbours, and add that wherever they went their own rites were a sufficient separation.

debates.question: Why is Christ called our peace rather than our peacemaker?

sides.position: Because it is he himself and not merely what he did
Because here alone, against the prince of peace who gives peace, his own nature is the actual tie of unity
Because those outside him are therefore at variance with God, which is at once assurance and rebuke

debates.question: What is the middle wall of partition?

sides.position: The temple barrier itself, dividing the court of the Gentiles from the court of Israel under an inscription forbidding a Gentile to pass
The ceremonial law, so called by allusion to that partition
The whole distinction that Jewish laws and customs made, the allusion being less precise, with the practice of living apart behind a river or wall offered as an alternative

debates.question: What does the enmity stand in apposition to?

sides.position: Either to the wall of partition or to the law of commandments, the general sense being little affected
To the wall, the enmity between Jew and Gentile simply being the partition; it is doubtful that it is the object of the verb for abolishing at all

outliers.note: Alone illustrates the abolished badges from his own century, setting circumcision, sacrifices, washings and forbidden foods beside the white and the red cross that distinguished the French from the Burgundians.
Alone turns the phrase in his flesh into a doctrinal marker, observing that nobody would say of a mere moral teacher that he accomplished a result by his flesh.

themes: he is our peace, who hath made both one
access by one Spirit unto the Father

19.pericope_label: Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God; And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone; In whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord: In whom ye also are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit.

schools.summary: Separate the two words for the outsider: the first names foreigners in a state as opposed to citizens, the second guests in a private family as opposed to its members, or, put another way, the alien and the half-alien resident. Fill in what such standing meant at Athens — a resident stranger could live and trade undisturbed but had no voice in the public deliberations and no part in the management of the state, could not transact business in his own name, and had to choose a citizen as patron to guard him against injustice. Observe that the sojourner's nearer position sharpened rather than softened the exclusion, and that the two replacements answer the two exclusions term for term, fellow-citizens to stranger and household to foreigner, because the unit in ancient law is always the family. On the foundation, hold it impossible to take the prophets here as those of the Old Testament, on the order of the two nouns, the comparison with two later passages in the epistle, and the stress on present against past; then canvass three senses of the foundation of the apostles and prophets and adopt with most ancient authorities the one that makes the men themselves the foundation, since Paul here calls Christ not the foundation but the corner-stone. Note the article missing before the word for building, so that ordinary Greek idiom asks for each several building rather than all the building, and that the participle for fitly framed together looks to be the apostle's own coinage.

Take the word for foundation to mean doctrine, since no patriarchs or pious kings are named here but only those who held the office of teachers; make this the mark by which a true church is distinguished from a false, and press the question against those who rest on the contrivances of men. Then guard the other side: strictly Christ alone is the foundation, supporting the whole church and serving as the rule and standard of faith, and he is the foundation on which the church is built by the preaching of doctrine, which is why the prophets and apostles are called builders. Ask what will then become of Peter, and answer from the passage where the apostle calls himself a wise master-builder who laid the foundation for another to build on. Order the two verbs at the close: first the fitting-together, believers accommodating themselves to one another, for otherwise there is no building but a confused mass, and the chief part of that symmetry is unity of faith; increase only follows. Add that the church is a building compact together, its parts joined by agreement and knit in love, proportioned for the strength of the whole.

Read the whole chapter as a city holding rights by charter, in which an uncircumcised God-fearer might dwell in the land as one who rents but never owns, while believing Gentiles are now incorporated with believing Jews. Take the foundation as the doctrine taught by the prophets in the Old Testament and the apostles in the New, and explain the corner-stone as the large stone laid at an angle to form part of the two walls that meet there. Then refuse the popular guess that the apostle glances at the temple of Diana, insisting the Jerusalem temple is in view throughout, since that alone could be called a habitation of God, where he dwelt between the cherubim and the worship was such as he had himself prescribed.

debates.question: Are the prophets of the foundation those of the Old Testament?

sides.position: No: the order of the two nouns, the comparison with two later passages, and the stress on present against past forbid it
Yes, the phrase covering revealed doctrine at large, whether given through prophet or apostle
Yes: the prophets of the Old Testament and the apostles of the New, who agree in laying the one foundation ministerially
Yes: the doctrine taught by the prophets in the Old Testament and the apostles in the New

debates.question: In what sense are the apostles and prophets a foundation?

sides.position: Themselves the foundation, the reading of most ancient authorities, since Christ is here the corner-stone and not the foundation
Not the men but the doctrine, since Christ alone strictly supports the church and is the rule and standard of faith
The doctrines they taught, laid as the basis on which the church rests — not philosophy, tradition, human laws or antiquity

debates.question: Should the clause be rendered all the building or every building?

sides.position: Every, or each several, building: the best manuscripts omit the article and ordinary Greek idiom requires it
All the building, the sense demanding it, though every act of building is the one other possible rendering

outliers.note: Alone denies that the prophets of the foundation are those of the Old Testament, against three other commentators here, and alone observes that the corner-stone relation proved too slight for the apostle, who leaves it for the body and its head.
Alone refuses the popular supposition that the apostle glances at the temple of Diana, insisting that the Jerusalem temple is in view because that alone could be called a habitation of God.

themes: the foundation of the apostles and prophets
an habitation of God through the Spirit
